135: Heavy advertising: +20% demand at all your businesses for 15 days.
137: Better service: +6 reputation at all your businesses.
139: Bargaining power: unit cost drops 10% for 30 days.
140: Hand out samples in the park
141: You give away products at the park fair: more people get to know your brands (+8 awareness at all your businesses).
143: The neighbors tell you what price they'd pay (the one that maximizes your profit) and they like being asked (+2 reputation).
145: Your brand on the court: +5 reputation at all your businesses and +25% demand at beach shops for 7 days.

147: Some free time: you sell what you catch at the harbor market. Best at dawn and at sunset.
163: Sunny day: the beach fills up and burgers sell more.
165: Partly cloudy skies: a normal day for selling.
167: Cloudy day: more people want a hot coffee and the beach is emptier.
169: It's raining: fewer people on the street, but coffee soars and the beach empties. Outdoor stands sell less.
171: Heat wave! The beach is packed with tourists, but nobody wants hot coffee and perishables spoil faster.
173: Storm! Almost nobody goes out: stands and the beach barely sell. Covered megastores hold up better.
175: Price × units sold. It's what comes in from sales before subtracting any cost.
177: What the goods you sold cost you. Calculated with the average inventory cost.
179: Revenue − cost of goods sold. Gross margin is that profit divided by revenue.
181: Variable costs grow with each unit (goods). Fixed costs are paid whether you sell or not (rent, salaries, managers).
183: Price − variable cost per unit. It's what each sale contributes to cover fixed costs.
185: Daily units you need to sell to cover fixed costs: fixed costs ÷ contribution margin. You'll see it in Market.
187: How much demand drops when you raise the price. With elasticity 2, raising the price 10% lowers demand by about 20%. The Market curve shows the price that maximizes profit.
189: How much demand changes with the economy. Premium drops a lot in a recession; budget quality is an inferior good and sells MORE in a recession.
191: Premium costs more but lets you charge more, improves reputation and makes customers less price-sensitive.
193: Marketing works, but each extra dollar brings in less than the one before. The same happens when you open many branches of one product (cannibalization).
195: The more you buy, the better price your supplier gives you (volume discount). Your own factory cuts cost by 30% if you sell enough.
197: With many branches, corporate overhead appears and grows faster than the number of stores.
199: Making what you sell yourself (your own factory). High fixed cost: only worth it with lots of volume.
201: Little inventory = lost sales. Lots of inventory = storage cost and waste. Choose your days of inventory carefully.
203: If a market is very profitable, competitors arrive and take your customers. In a recession some close. You can acquire them.
205: Buying a competitor removes rivalry and gives you their store. The premium over their assets is called goodwill.
207: Prices rise over time: your costs, salaries and rents too. If you don't raise your prices, your real margin shrinks.
209: The economy goes through expansion, boom, recession and recovery. It affects demand, inflation and interest rates.
211: The central bank raises the rate when there's inflation. That makes your loans more expensive and pays more on bonds.
213: Borrowing multiplies growth, but interest is due even if you sell little. More debt = higher rate.
215: Loans are paid in equal monthly installments that include interest and principal.
217: What you invest in branches and factories is spread as an expense over 5 years. No cash goes out, but it lowers profit and taxes.
219: Interest and depreciation are subtracted before taxes, so you pay less tax.
221: If you lose money one month, that loss is deducted from future profits before paying taxes.
223: If you sell a branch you only get back half its book value. What you invested won't come back: decide looking forward.
225: Idle money could earn interest in bonds. If your business earns less than bonds, you're losing money even while making a profit.
227: Return on each branch's investment, on your equity and on your total assets. They compare how much you earn with how much you put in.
229: Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization. Measures how much the business operation generates.
231: Net profit − (equity × cost of capital). If positive, you create wealth above the opportunity cost.
233: Your company is worth roughly annual EBITDA × multiple + cash − debt. Multiples rise in a boom and fall in a recession.
235: You can have negative cash for a while (overdraft) at a very high interest rate. If you stay over the limit for many days, you go bankrupt.
237: A manager costs a fixed salary, but automatically adjusts staff and inventory for their line.
239: Expected value = sum of (probability × outcome). Two options with the same expected value can carry very different risks: the game's dilemmas show you the odds so you can compare.
241: Losing $100 hurts more than winning $100 feels good. That's why it's hard to cut a losing business or break a streak: recognize it and decide with numbers.
243: An unethical shortcut (bribes, cartels, shady goods) can save money today, but if it's discovered the fine and the lost reputation cost much more.
245: What the company spends on its owner's image (clothes, accessories). It's an operating expense: it lowers profit like any other.
247: Investing in systems (ERP, shared services, AI) lowers the cost of coordinating many branches. It's how you keep growing without corporate overhead eating your profit.
249: Stocks earn more than bonds on average, but they go up and down every day and fall hard in a recession. Higher expected return always comes with more risk.
251: Agreeing on prices with the competition raises both margins at the customer's expense. It's illegal: antitrust authorities punish it with huge fines.
